reference.source: Textbook of Pediatric Rheumatology / ILAR & PRINTO criteria
clinicalPearls: Under the ILAR system, diagnosis requires arthritis with psoriasis, or arthritis with at least two of dactylitis, nail pitting or onycholysis, and a first-degree relative with psoriasis
Arthritis often precedes the skin disease in children, so psoriasis may not be evident at presentation
Dactylitis (sausage digit) reflects combined joint and tenosynovial inflammation and is a useful clue
Nail changes such as pitting and onycholysis support the diagnosis even when skin psoriasis is subtle or absent
A bimodal pattern is described, with a younger group resembling oligoarticular disease (antinuclear-antibody positive, uveitis risk) and an older group resembling spondyloarthritis
Chronic anterior uveitis surveillance is required, particularly in younger antinuclear-antibody-positive children
Treatment follows JIA principles with NSAIDs, intra-articular corticosteroids, methotrexate and TNF inhibition for resistant disease
reference.pathophysiology: Juvenile psoriatic arthritis is an immune-mediated inflammatory arthropathy sharing mechanisms with both juvenile idiopathic arthritis and the spondyloarthritis spectrum. Activation of T cells and cytokine pathways, including tumour necrosis factor and the interleukin-23/interleukin-17 axis, drives synovitis, enthesitis and the tenosynovial inflammation responsible for dactylitis, alongside the epidermal hyperproliferation of psoriasis and nail disease. The condition is heterogeneous, with a younger subgroup behaving like early-onset oligoarticular disease and an older subgroup showing entheseal and axial features.
additionalDifferentials: Other JIA subtypes, particularly oligoarticular and enthesitis-related arthritis
additionalInvestigations: Careful skin and nail examination for psoriasis, pitting and onycholysis
Antinuclear antibody to stratify uveitis risk
Inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein)
Joint ultrasound or MRI to confirm synovitis, tenosynovitis and enthesitis
HLA-B27 in older children with axial or entheseal features
Slit-lamp ophthalmology assessment for uveitis surveillance
Radiographs of affected joints in established disease
redFlags: Silent sight-threatening uveitis in younger antinuclear-antibody-positive children
Axial or sacroiliac involvement suggesting a spondyloarthritis phenotype
Rapidly erosive or destructive joint disease
Systemic upset or night pain suggesting infection or malignancy
reference.prognosis: Outcomes vary with phenotype; some children have limited disease while others develop persistent or erosive arthritis. As with other JIA subtypes, early treatment and diligent uveitis surveillance improve long-term joint and visual outcomes.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because psoriasis is not yet apparent, when arthritis often comes first
Overlooking subtle nail changes and dactylitis
Neglecting uveitis surveillance in younger antinuclear-antibody-positive children
Failing to recognise an evolving spondyloarthritis phenotype in older children
Delaying disease-modifying therapy in progressive disease
references: ILAR classification of juvenile idiopathic arthritis
Consensus guidance on juvenile psoriatic arthritis
management: Intra-articular corticosteroid injections for active oligoarticular disease, with NSAIDs for symptomatic joint and entheseal relief
Methotrexate as first-line disease-modifying therapy for persistent or polyarticular disease and for dactylitis
Escalate to TNF inhibitors or IL-17/IL-23-axis biologics for methotrexate-refractory joint, axial or skin disease
Treat cutaneous psoriasis and nail disease with topical therapy in coordination with dermatology
Undertake regular slit-lamp uveitis surveillance, particularly in younger antinuclear-antibody-positive children
Provide physiotherapy and occupational therapy to preserve joint range and function
Coordinate multidisciplinary paediatric rheumatology, dermatology and ophthalmology care with structured transition to adult services
